section_summary: This section completes a detailed questionnaire on Japan’s narcotics-control system, covering import and export certificates, transit, storage, recordkeeping, inspections, penalties, and international enforcement cooperation. It then documents growing American and Canadian concern over Japanese-manufactured morphine and heroin smuggled to the Pacific Coast, particularly aboard the Venice Maru and President Madison. Correspondence and reports criticize the Osaka police’s failure to trace regulated narcotics and seek to centralize future investigations through the American Embassy in Tokyo; the final pages contain original and duplicate copies of supporting reports, interviews, and a purchaser list.

subfiles.title: Questionnaire on Japanese narcotics laws and administrative controls
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Continuation of a systematic account of Japan’s laws and procedures governing narcotic drugs.
subfiles.summary: The questionnaire describes Japan’s import and export certificate system, customs procedures, transit rules, bonded warehouses, storage, prescriptions, reports, inspections, illicit-traffic enforcement, and penalties. It identifies the Minister for Home Affairs as the principal certificate and reporting authority and explains Japan’s quarterly reporting to the Permanent Central Board at Geneva. It also notes the 1928 and 1929 informal arrangements for exchanging enforcement information with the United States.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Tokyo despatch No. 398 and narcotics questionnaire
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a Tokyo Embassy despatch and summary of narcotics laws in Japan and the Mandated Islands.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends the Treasury Department, for the Commissioner of Narcotics, a copy of despatch No. 398 and its enclosed questionnaire. The enclosure summarizes laws and regulations controlling narcotics traffic in Japan and the Mandated Islands.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet concerning a proposed Chinese Yellow Book
subfiles.from: Gilbert, Geneva
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram about a proposed Chinese publication on illicit narcotics traffic and Japanese involvement.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers researchers to another file containing Geneva telegram No. 308. It records that the Chinese Minister proposed circulating a Yellow Book at the next Assembly meeting describing unlawful narcotics imports into China and Manchuria, with particular attention to the alleged Japanese role.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet concerning Japanese participation in the Persian opium trade
subfiles.from: Wadsworth, Persia
subfiles.about: Refers to a despatch on Japanese interests in Persian opium and other commodities.
subfiles.summary: The filing note directs the reader to another despatch concerning Japanese participation in Persian commerce. Its brief description states that Japan purchased a substantial portion of Persia’s opium.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 277: Tracing the origin of narcotic drugs
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Recommends routing investigations of suspected Japanese narcotics through the Embassy rather than local consular and police channels.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the American Consul at Kobe cannot obtain useful assistance from local police in tracing drugs seized from vessels arriving in the United States. He proposes that American customs officials send labels, photographs, and samples directly to the Embassy, which would request an investigation from the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Telegram instructing the Tokyo Embassy on narcotics investigations
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Orders an inquiry into duplicated American investigations and prescribes centralized handling of future Japanese narcotics cases.
subfiles.summary: The Department cites increasing quantities of Japanese morphine on the Pacific Coast and the unanswered request concerning the Venice Maru seizure at Seattle. It directs the Embassy to determine, without approaching Japanese authorities, what the Treasury Attaché did in the Venice Maru and subsequent cases. Future customs requests are to be referred through the Embassy and the established direct-exchange channel with the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: Grew’s reply concerning Venice Maru and President Madison investigations
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports unsuccessful Osaka investigations and recommends raising the matter with Japan’s Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Attaché had requested investigations in the Venice Maru and President Madison cases through the American Consul at Kobe, but Osaka authorities produced no results. Grew states that future cases will be referred to the Embassy and suggests that higher-level intervention by the Foreign Minister may be necessary.

subfiles.title: Instruction to copy narcotics correspondence to the State Department
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs consular officers to provide confidential copies of their narcotics correspondence with Treasury Attachés.
subfiles.summary: Hull instructs all American consular officers in Japan to send the Department confidential copies of correspondence addressed to Treasury Attachés concerning narcotic drugs. The order is intended to improve State Department oversight of such investigations.

subfiles.title: Anslinger covering letter enclosing Sharman’s report on Japanese morphine
subfiles.from: H. J. Anslinger, Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.to: Stuart J. Fuller, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a Canadian report on a Japanese offer to supply narcotics and asks how broadly the information should be used.
subfiles.summary: Anslinger encloses C. H. L. Sharman’s March 27 letter for Fuller’s confidential information. He proposes telling Sharman that Japanese cooperation has been inadequate and advising him to withhold the intelligence until a confirming case has been successfully developed.

subfiles.title: Sharman letter on a Kobe narcotics-smuggling proposal
subfiles.from: C. H. L. Sharman, Chief, Narcotic Division, Ottawa
subfiles.to: H. J. Anslinger, Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Reports a Kobe supplier’s letter proposing methods for smuggling morphine, heroin, and cocaine into Canada and the United States.
subfiles.summary: Sharman reproduces extracts from K. Yuki’s letter to a Vancouver resident, which recommends concealing drugs in double-soled shoes or shipping them in cans disguised as ordinary cargo. The letter includes prices for morphine, heroin, and cocaine and claims successful earlier shipments to China and India. Canadian officers are continuing the correspondence through their informer while considering whether disclosure to foreign or Japanese authorities would expose him.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on investigations of illicit narcotics traffic involving Japan
subfiles.from: Stuart J. Fuller, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese narcotics seizures, deficient Japanese cooperation, and poor coordination among American agencies.
subfiles.summary: Fuller surveys major Pacific Coast seizures and the unsuccessful efforts to secure Japanese investigations through the direct-exchange agreement. He recounts contacts with Kusama, Grew’s despatch, the conflicting activities of the Commissioner of Narcotics, Customs, consuls, and the Treasury Attaché, and the risk of embarrassment at the Opium Advisory Committee. The memorandum recommends temporarily routing all investigation requests through the American Embassy in Tokyo and obtaining copies of consular correspondence with Treasury Attachés.

subfiles.title: Tabulation of Japanese drugs and ships
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Lists principal American seizures of drugs associated with Japanese vessels, labels, or manufacturers.
subfiles.summary: The table records seizures at Honolulu, Seattle, Tacoma, Scappoose, and Los Angeles between February 1932 and February 1933. It identifies the Asama Maru, Venice Maru, President Madison, Yogi Maru, and Akagisan Maru and lists patent medicines, morphine, and cocaine, including manufacturer labels and reported quantities.

subfiles.title: Anslinger covering letter enclosing Smith’s Pacific Coast report
subfiles.from: H. J. Anslinger, Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.to: Stuart J. Fuller, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a district supervisor’s report on Japanese morphine trafficking.
subfiles.summary: Anslinger sends Fuller a confidential copy of Harry D. Smith’s April 14 report from San Francisco. The enclosure concerns Japanese smugglers and distributors operating along the Pacific Coast.

subfiles.title: Smith letter on Japanese narcotics networks on the Pacific Coast
subfiles.from: Harry D. Smith, District Supervisor, U.S. Narcotic Service
subfiles.to: H. J. Anslinger, Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Argues that recent West Coast cases reveal a large Japanese morphine-importing organization requiring broader investigation.
subfiles.summary: Smith reports that abundant Japanese morphine has reduced illicit prices and cites related arrests and seizures in Los Angeles, Seattle, Portland, and Oregon. He identifies Mayeda, whose cable registry was Kojitaka, as a principal importer and mentions an Osaka contact using the registry Kawatatsu. He urges coordinated investigation with Japanese authorities and increased attention by customs collectors at Pacific ports.

subfiles.title: Draft letter proposing centralized investigation requests to Japan
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests Treasury cooperation in routing Japanese narcotics investigations through the State Department and American Embassy.
subfiles.summary: The draft reviews Pacific Coast seizures, unanswered approaches under the direct-exchange agreement, and ineffective parallel inquiries by Customs and the Treasury Attaché. It warns that overlapping American approaches could allow Japan to justify its lack of cooperation before the Opium Advisory Committee, as France had done in an earlier case. The Department asks that the Commissioner of Narcotics submit investigation requests through State and that the Treasury Attaché at Kobe contact Japanese authorities only through the Embassy in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal of Customs reports on Japanese narcotics
subfiles.from: F. A. Birgfeld, U.S. Treasury Department
subfiles.about: Transmits Customs and Treasury Attaché reports concerning Japanese heroin and morphine investigations.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department responds to Fuller’s request for information about twenty-two ounces of heroin seized at Seattle in January 1931 and other drugs apparently of Japanese origin. It encloses Melvin L. Hanks’s September 1932 report and Martin G. Scott’s confidential January 1933 report with their attachments for use by American officers attending a forthcoming European opium meeting.

subfiles.title: Hanks report on tracing Japanese heroin and morphine to Osaka manufacturers
subfiles.from: Melvin L. Hanks, Customs Agent at Large, Seattle
subfiles.about: Examines evidence linking Seattle heroin and Venice Maru morphine seizures to pharmaceutical producers in Osaka.
subfiles.summary: Hanks reviews a 1931 heroin seizure labeled Japan Pharmaceutical Establishment and Scott’s inquiry into licensed and suspected Osaka manufacturers. He then describes sixty tins of morphine seized from the Venice Maru, their Dai Nihon markings, defaced identification stickers, and the arrest of chief steward Tadauki Ito and three others. He requests microscopic examination of the remaining labels and sends photographs to Kobe for checking with Osaka police.

subfiles.title: Scott report on failed Osaka police investigations
subfiles.from: Martin G. Scott, Treasury Attaché, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports that Osaka police failed to trace the President Madison and Venice Maru morphine despite Japan’s strict narcotics records.
subfiles.summary: Scott recounts requests to trace fourteen bottles from the President Madison and sixty tins from the Venice Maru. He dismisses the police explanations as implausible because labels, serial numbers, manufacturers, and regulated sales records should have made the drugs traceable. Concluding that local approaches are useless, he recommends diplomatic pressure through the State Department and warns that Osaka may be a major source of narcotics smuggled into the United States.

subfiles.title: Donovan letter on referring Osaka narcotics cases to the Embassy
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Agrees that Osaka police investigations are ineffective and states that future cases will be referred to the Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Donovan acknowledges Scott’s request concerning the Venice Maru and the earlier President Madison case. He calls the Osaka police handling farcical, asserts that the sellers could readily be identified, and says future cases will go to the Embassy as the Ambassador suggested.

subfiles.title: Dorsz memorandum of interview with Osaka Prefectural Police
subfiles.from: Edmund J. Dorsz, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Records an unsuccessful interview with Osaka police chiefs about morphine seized from the President Madison and Venice Maru.
subfiles.summary: Miyata told Dorsz that fifty bottles bearing the President Madison label’s license number had been accounted for to police satisfaction, while inquiries outside Osaka Prefecture remained incomplete. He evaded questions about total production and claimed that the Venice Maru case could not proceed without a sample or label. Dorsz concluded that the interview yielded little useful information.

subfiles.title: Translation of Osaka morphine sales under serial number 5525
subfiles.from: Osaka Prefectural Police
subfiles.about: Lists the seller and purchasers of fifty bottles of morphine hydrochloride bearing serial number 5525.
subfiles.summary: The translation identifies Usaburo Morishita as seller and states that the morphine was bottled at the Osaka Hygienic Laboratory on July 8, 1932. It lists seven purchasers in Osaka Prefecture, their addresses, purchase dates, and quantities totaling fifty bottles.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Hanks report on Osaka narcotics manufacturers
subfiles.from: Melvin L. Hanks, Customs Agent at Large, Seattle
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the report linking Seattle heroin and Venice Maru morphine to Osaka pharmaceutical sources.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate repeats Hanks’s account of the 1931 heroin seizure and the investigation of Osaka manufacturers. It also repeats the details of the Venice Maru morphine tins, the defaced factory-identification stickers, and the plan to have labels examined and checked by the Treasury Attaché and Osaka police.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Scott report on Osaka police noncooperation
subfiles.from: Martin G. Scott, Treasury Attaché, Kobe
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of Scott’s report criticizing the Osaka police response to two morphine cases.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate recounts the unsuccessful attempts to trace morphine seized from the President Madison and Venice Maru. Scott argues that Japan’s detailed sales controls made the police excuses untenable and concludes that only diplomatic pressure through the State Department is likely to produce cooperation.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Donovan letter on Embassy referral
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy stating that future narcotics cases should be referred to the Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Donovan again characterizes Osaka police handling of the Venice Maru and President Madison cases as farcical. He says the police could identify the sellers if they wished and confirms that future cases will be sent to the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Dorsz memorandum of the Osaka police interview
subfiles.from: Edmund J. Dorsz, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the interview record concerning license number 5525 and the two shipboard seizures.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Miyata’s assertion that fifty bottles sold in Osaka under the relevant license number had been satisfactorily accounted for. It also repeats his evasive answers on production and his demand for a sample or label before investigating the Venice Maru seizure. Dorsz again records the interview as unsuccessful.

subfiles.title: Duplicate translation of Osaka morphine sales under serial number 5525
subfiles.from: Osaka Prefectural Police
subfiles.about: Duplicate list of the seller and purchasers of fifty bottles of morphine hydrochloride.
subfiles.summary: The page repeats the translated record identifying the seller, the Osaka Hygienic Laboratory, the bottling date, and serial number 5525. It lists the seven purchasers, their Osaka-area addresses, dates, and quantities totaling fifty bottles.
